how easily someone else could check that this copy is what its source published, unaltered
Connection
how easily someone else could check this link: that this payment, vote, office or person is the one meant
Testimony
how easily someone else could check what a witness says
Subject match
how easily someone else could check that this record is about this person or thing
A is easiest to check; D rests on a person's word. A grade never says whether something is true.
Undetermined
Undetermined: the record can't determine this from what your team holds, and the reason is always given. An answer, not an error.
Withheld
Withheld: something is here that you can't see, kept back by its source or by who may see it. That it exists is shown, never hidden.
Unrated
Unrated: not graded yet.
Nobody looked
Nobody looked: no one has searched for this yet. Not the same as “looked for, not found”.
Refused
Refused: Civicsmith won't do this. The reason says why, and what you can do instead.
Machine work
Machine work: made by the assistant or an automatic check, never by a member. It counts only once a member accepts it.
Another team's
Another team's: from another team's published case, recreated here. It counts only once your team accepts it.
Not yet evaluated
Not yet evaluated: no one in your team has judged this yet.
Accepted by our team
Accepted by our team: a member accepted it, with a reason you can open.
Flagged
Flagged: someone marked this for a second look.
Found by search
Found by search: Civicsmith matched these words in what your team holds. Nothing is recorded: a member records it, from its passage, with the usual act.
To do
To do: something only you can move forward.
Noticed
Noticed: something changed that you may want to know. Nothing is required of you.
Status
Status: where something you follow stands.
Working: not public; seen by your team's members.
Shared for review: named outsiders can read this draft until the owner stops sharing it.
Published: signed and public. It can be corrected by a new edition, never removed.
An answer is only as strong as the weakest thing it depends on: its weakest document copy and its least certain link, side by side, never merged.
A due date, counted on your team's local day. Open it to see the law or commitment it comes from and how the days were counted.
Hint · machine work: something the machine marked worth a look, with how it was found and out of how many. A lead, never a finding.
Hunch: a member's suspicion, labeled as one. Never evidence, and it never moves a finding.
Outward: this leaves your team's Civicsmith. Someone outside will see it.
Where you are: this band says who can see what you are working on.
Protected word: it protects members, so a change to it needs a second check before it shows.
Local name: the official name stays as it is, with an explanation in the member's language beside it.

What we look into
Our team looks into whether a government, an agency or a public body keeps its own rules and promises. We check what it says against its own records, and publish what the records show.
Every finding shows its source

Each finding we publish points to the passage it rests on: a page of a budget, a line of the minutes, a row of an office's own data. Open any finding in a published case and the passage opens with it, so you can read it yourself.
How strong the evidence is

Each piece of evidence carries a letter, A strongest to D weakest, and says why it has that letter: a copy fetched from the office's own website holds up better than one found elsewhere. A finding is never stronger than its weakest piece, and where something isn't known, the case says so instead of guessing.
What we publish, and who stands behind it
A case is published only when a member signs it. Once published it is never changed quietly: a correction comes as a new edition, and the earlier one stays readable with the correction beside it.
Have something for us?
Anyone can hand us documents or a tip without an account. The page says what will happen to what you give, and you decide how much to tell us about yourself.
Taking part
Members join by an invitation from one of our administrators. If you would like to take part, ask a member you know, or tell us through “Have something for us?”. Members sign in from our page.

words.en: Civicsmith can include an AI assistant, built on Anthropic's Claude. Members ask it, in everyday words, to find, read and check things in your team's material. Privacy and the law
words.note: adopted from screens-entry's own rows; DEC-259: reworded

words.en: Civicsmith keeps your team's unpublished work private, from the public and from the people you look into. But a court order your team can't defeat can still require anything not public to be shown, such as members' notes, sources and hidden projects. Much work never draws such an order, and journalists, lawyers and auditors may have protections others lack.

words.en: Your handle

The record shows your handle on your work. Choose it with care: it can't be changed after you join, and no one else can ever take it. It needn't be your legal name. Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, 2 to 41 of them, starting with a letter or digit. Choosing a handle: a name people know lends your work credibility and lets reporters reach you, but puts it on public cases; a pen name shields you from pressure, while the administrators still know who you are.

Before you choose a password: who controls your team's Civicsmith

Whoever can sign in to the hosting account your team's Civicsmith runs in (its Cloudflare account) controls it. They can replace the one-time password, claim it again, read everything in it and lock everyone else out, and no vote of the team's administrators can stop them.
Use a team account for it, not anyone's personal login.
Add at least one other trusted person to that account.
Where possible, let someone other than the team's administrators hold it.
The same account is the way back in if the password you choose is lost: whoever holds it can open the way for your team's Civicsmith to be claimed again.
If the one-time password may have been seen, replace it: follow the guide “Replace the one-time password” in your team's Civicsmith, on its first page and in its members and keys section.
If you cannot sign in
Your team's administrators can help you: ask one of them for a reset link.
If none of them can sign in either, whoever holds your team's hosting account can open the way back in for them.

What a spot-check does

A calculation counts what a source records, such as the reports the city marked closed. A spot-check tests whether the record matches what is really there: members visit a random sample of the counted items and record what they find.
Why the sample is random, and recorded

Civicsmith draws the sample from a recorded seed. Anyone, including the city or a reporter, can repeat the draw and get exactly the same items, so no one could have picked the easy or the damning ones.
words.note: adopted from screens-investigate's own rows; DEC-257: reworded

words.en: What the result says

The share of visited items that matched, and an exact range for the whole set. The range is what the sample can honestly support: the true share for all items is very likely inside it. A larger sample gives a narrower range: about 13 points either way for 40 items, about 9 for 100.
What it does not say

Nothing certain about any one item no one visited. Nothing about items outside the set that was drawn from. Items members could not judge are counted apart and named, never guessed; the estimate assumes they are like the rest, and says so.
Each visit is evidence

Each visit is recorded as the testimony of the member who made it. A photo, where the member took one, lets others see what was there; the member's account counts with or without one. A finding resting on a spot-check shows the draw, every visit, and the range.

Work done in Civicsmith can matter. Checking whether officials and agencies keep their own rules can show money misspent, deadlines ignored or promises broken, and a published case can lead to a correction, an audit or a lawsuit. People and organizations a team looks into sometimes go to court to see the work behind it.
The explanation is always one tap away for every member. You choose whether members are also told when they join and the first time they record something not public.
Connect a tool
Your team's Civicsmith is set up.
Once chosen, the step says: “{done}” Then it opens Home.
Hold your government to its own word

Civicsmith is free software for a team of people who want to know whether their government is doing what it must: obeying the laws that bind it and the court decisions it is subject to, keeping the rules it set for itself and the promises it made.

The team gathers the records, works out what they show, and publishes what it finds in a form anyone can check. Neighborhood groups, newsrooms, professional associations and offices checking their own work all use it the same way.
Start a team's Civicsmith
See what teams have published
How a team uses it

Gather the records. Members collect the records that bear on the question, from wherever they were published: the city's minutes, budgets, contracts and letters; state and federal regulations and reports; court decisions; the press releases and filings of private firms. Civicsmith keeps each one exactly as its source published it, with where and when it came from. Together these are the team's record.
Ask a question. In the team’s own words: “{example}”

Weigh the evidence. Members mark the passages of the record that bear on the question. Civicsmith grades each passage by how easily a stranger could check it, from a copy fetched straight from the office down to one person's word.
Reach a finding. The team's answer to its question, resting on named evidence, with how strong that evidence is. A hunch is kept as a hunch; it never becomes a finding.
Publish a case. The findings, their evidence and their strength, published together and signed by a member of the team. Anyone can read it and check it without asking the team.
What a team gets
Its own copy of Civicsmith. Each team runs its own copy, in a Cloudflare account the team controls. Nobody else holds the team's work, the people who make Civicsmith included.
Findings anyone can check. Every finding points to the passages it rests on and says how strong that evidence is, so a reader never has to take the team's word for it.

Help for people who have never done this. A guide walks each common job step by step, from asking an office for a record to publishing a case. An AI assistant is optional: it answers only from what the team holds, says where it looked, and never concludes, signs or sends. Everything works without it.
Free software. Civicsmith costs nothing. The team pays Cloudflare $5 a month for the account its copy runs in.
What Civicsmith does not do
It takes no side on what policy should be. It asks only whether the government kept its word.
It gives legal information, never legal advice.
It publishes nothing a member has not signed, and it sends no email.
Open it as any reader does: each finding, its evidence and how strong it is, and a way to check the signature without asking the team.

Your team's Civicsmith has its own address, and you sign in there, not here: civicsmith.org holds no accounts. Ask your team for its address, or find it on your team's own website.

words.en: For a team that has decided to create its own copy. This page says what you need, who should hold what, what happens step by step, and what it costs. Reading it takes five minutes; the installer takes about twenty.
Is it right for your team?

It fits if your team wants to find out whether a government, agency or public body is keeping the laws, rules and promises that bind it, and to show what the records say in a way others can check. It does not fit a team that wants a place to post opinions, or one that needs a lawyer's advice: Civicsmith gives neither.

A Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan, $5 a month, with a payment method. Cloudflare is the company whose computers will run your team's copy. Open the account in your team's name, not a person's.
About twenty minutes at a computer.

Nothing else. No server, no company, no technical knowledge, and no Claude account: the assistant is optional, and members connect their own accounts later if they want it. The installer asks you two things and does the rest.
Decide first: who holds the Cloudflare account

Whoever can sign in to that account controls your team's Civicsmith. They can read everything in it, and they are the way back in if every administrator is ever locked out. Agree as a team on who that is, and add a second trusted person to the account, so it never depends on one person. The installer says this again at the moment it matters.
What happens, step by step

You choose a short name and your places. The short name is a fixed label in your team's addresses and beside every signature; it never changes. The places are the city, county and state whose rules apply to you. Places ready now: {places}. For each, Civicsmith already holds the local facts it works from: its offices, where its records are published, its deadlines and its holidays.
Cloudflare asks your permission, on its own page, to let the installer create your team's copy in your account.
The installer puts your team's Civicsmith in place and checks it. About ten minutes. If a step stops, the installer says why and what to do; a stop before setup has begun creates nothing.
You claim it. The installer shows you a one-time password; you use it once, choose your own password, and become the team's first administrator. More administrators can be added later.
You set it up. Your team's name, the languages its members use, and whether members may use the assistant. All of it can be changed later.
You invite members. Each gets a link you send yourself, by whatever means you trust; Civicsmith sends no email. Each member chooses the name their work will carry.

$5 a month to Cloudflare for the account. If members use the assistant, its use is paid to Anthropic by whoever connected the account that serves it, and the team can set limits. Nothing is paid to the people who make Civicsmith.

words.en: Dividing does not remove anything. Every leg this question rests on gets a home on one of the children, including any leg that cuts against you, and this question stays on the record as the divided parent, recording where each leg went. Each child names this parent and every sibling, and when a child is published it names them to its readers. If you mean to drop material rather than re-home it, remove the citation, with a reason, instead.

words.en: Grouping says these reasons are enough on their own to carry your answer. Your answer's strength is then taken from the strongest team rather than from its weakest single reason, so your name and the time go on each team you make and stay there until that team's reasons change. Nothing is hidden: every reason stays visible under the team you put it in, and a published case carries each team and what it reached inside the signed bytes, so a reader can check whether they really were enough on their own. Leaving the reasons ungrouped is always available, and is read as no stronger than the weakest one.

words.en: What co-attestation answers: when did these bytes exist? It asks an independent timestamp authority to record that this capture's exact bytes existed no later than a fixed instant. What it does not answer: whether the document is TRUE, whether its source is authoritative, or how close it stands to the fact you are citing it for. A secondhand report that is co-attested is still a secondhand report. What it is worth: it strengthens a Grade {ceiling} capture toward evidentiary weight. It never reaches Grade {unreachable} — that needs a chain-of-custody web archive this surface cannot produce.

The listing rule

civicsmith.org lists every team whose administrators choose to list it. We decline or remove a listing only when it (1) is not a team using Civicsmith, or is advertising or spam; (2) pretends to be another team, person or office; (3) publishes something a court has ordered removed, or that is unlawful to publish; or (4) aims at a private person rather than at a government's work: their home, family or private life. We never decline or remove a listing for a team's views, its conclusions, or whom it holds to account, public officials and companies included. We tell the team which part of this rule applies and why; once it is fixed, the team can ask again.

Not offered, because they share what is sent to them: VirusTotal uploads, Jotti, Hybrid Analysis, and the public modes of ANY.RUN, Joe Sandbox and urlscan.io. An address check never sends the full address to anyone new: only checks that send a scrambled fragment, or Cloudflare's own. words.en: The Workers Containers permission, which the setup asks for. It installs the built-in file scanner and safe view: without it, files are kept and shown but not scanned, and a high-risk file opens only in its safe view once one can be made. Everything else installs either way.

words.en: What happens, and what we can and cannot see

words.en: The installer asks Cloudflare to show you a permission screen naming exactly what it may do in your account: install the software, set up its storage, and set up the containers for the file scanner and safe view. You approve it on Cloudflare's own page, and you can revoke it any time from your dashboard.
words.note: DEC-338: B323 5: bio-plane/public/newgroup/index.html (the invitation page): paragraph

words.en: That permission passes through the installer for the seconds the installation takes, is stored nowhere, and is never seen by a person. After setup, nothing your team does routes through the installer, or its publisher, at all.
words.note: DEC-338: B323 5: bio-plane/public/newgroup/index.html (the invitation page): paragraph

words.en: Prefer that nothing pass through the installer even once? The manual path is documented and permanently supported, using only the Cloudflare dashboard. It exists so your team could stand its Civicsmith up even if the publisher of Civicsmith releases disappeared tomorrow. Find it in the project documentation.

words.en: the source team is named by its slug, and this manifest states {value}
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: A member takes every act that commits the team: declaring a standard, determining, assessing a consequence or a success, choosing an option, approving, sending, advancing or stopping a stage, resolving, closing.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: a procedure guide lists the routes the profile or the team knows for one kind of action, in its order and unranked, with the replies to expect and each route's citation; it is legal information, not legal advice, and never how the AI may behave: the AI's rules of conduct come only from the rules Bob approves, no guide can loosen them, and code checks that none does.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: A sentence that asserts a breach as the team's finding needs a live noncompliant determination.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: A version may be written for a particular audience (the violating party, the team's members, an oversight office, the public) or broadly for all.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Administrators, or members given the grant, have a translation workspace listing every interface word beside the team's language, gaps marked; the assistant drafts the missing ones as labeled drafts, a member who knows the language checks and adopts each, and without the assistant members type them.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Civicsmith takes no position on what policy should be, and does not rule on policy even when members or teams do.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Claims about a body rest on findings of the three kinds in §3 or on the team's own dated correspondence; statements about what the team itself is doing need neither.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Counsel may be briefed at any stage, for a claim or for the team's defense, without a determination
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Every plan for an infraction also offers the violating party the chance to fix and remediate: a notice saying what correcting the act and remedying its harm would look like, with the law's period or a time the team sets.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: No fact and no rule from the model's knowledge; every rule from the plane (system rules from affordances, the team's rules from its reads, jurisdiction rules from the profile, law's text from `standards`); "not held" at its level, with the act that would find it; quotes beside every summary
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: no reading guide was passed to this render: a guide is the team's or Civicsmith's, read for the kind of document a run reads by the run's caller, and with none this layer carries nothing to read for.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Outward acts are classed by what their text does: asking an office to examine something, seeking evidence (a records request, a request for comment), and enforcing the team's own request on its own dated record are never held back.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Suggested options come from reasoning over the matter, the routes the profile's guides list and the team's own earlier plans, never from a fixed catalog; the plan holds no costs, assignees or hours (members take up work themselves, rule 20).
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: The AI may read a document the team holds a few pages at a time, within a reading limit, and never one under a "no AI" limit.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: the fixed terms (the grades, "Undetermined", the queue's kinds, the acts' names) each carry a note on what they mean, so every language says the same thing; renaming words within a language stays out (option A), so cases read the same from team to team.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: the team's own local words are its to translate as ordinary words.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: The team's own writing (notes, questions, findings, notices) can be read in a member's language on request: the assistant drafts the translation, labeled "Machine translation · original in English", with the original one tap away; it never replaces the original.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: the plane's published catalog holds no {id} act, the one act through which a member asks to read the team's own writing in her language, so this layer carries no doctrine for work no draft can do.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: the plane's published catalog holds no {INTERFACE_TRANSLATION_ACT} act, the one act a run drafts the interface words a team's language lacks through, so this layer carries no doctrine for work no run can do.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: The signed statement is the team's, adopted by a member, and the record keeps that it began as a machine draft.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: The system is nonetheless prepared for stonewalling, retaliation, discrediting and legal harassment: every plan is checked for a branch that answers a hostile response; pressure against the team or its supporters is recorded as evidence wherever it arrives, and can open an inquiry of its own; lawful demands are complied with openly.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: this layer is INSTRUCTION. A draft is answered to the member who asked for it, labeled as machine work, and stored nowhere; it never rewrites the member's text, and what it reads is fenced by the modules that serve it. It becomes the team's only by a member's own acts, which refuse a machine. A run ignoring every word here gets past nothing.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: this layer is INSTRUCTION, and this pack reads no account, grant, keep-away setting or word list: which account serves the member, whether the team keeps the assistant away, which member is granted a language and which words a draft is given are read for each call by the modules that serve it. A draft is recorded apart, labeled as machine work, and becomes the team's wording only by a granted member's act. A run ignoring every word here gets past nothing.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: this layer is INSTRUCTION. Every act it names is refused or labeled by the module that performs it: a drafted statement is stored apart and labeled as machine work, and becomes the team's statement only by a member's signing act, which refuses a machine. A run ignoring every word here gets past nothing.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: What the team chose changes only by a member's act.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: What the team sends is checked against its record.
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Wherever a member writes in their own words, the assistant, when reachable, offers "Help me write this": it works only from what the member tells it and what the team holds, never adds a fact (for an observation it only helps word what the member saw), and its words arrive labeled "Draft · the assistant's, asked by" and the asking member's handle, saved only when the member keeps them.

words.en: With the member's suggestions switch off it works only from what the member typed; with it on it may also draw on what the team holds (rule 7).
words.note: DEC-355: B362, reviewed from code (K3930, K4066): "group" for the team written as "team"; American spelling (DEC-221)

words.en: Open a Cloudflare account and confirm its email
Your team's Civicsmith runs in this account, so open it for your team: use an email your team shares, not one person's own.
Go to dash.cloudflare.com/sign-up, enter the email and a password, and create the account. Cloudflare then emails that address: open the message and press its link to confirm it.
Nothing: opening the account is free.
Choose Workers Paid and add a payment method
Workers Paid is the Cloudflare plan that can run every part of your team's Civicsmith, the file scanner and the safe view for risky files included. The free plan can't.
In Cloudflare, open Workers & Pages, then Plans, and choose Workers Paid. Add a card or another payment method when Cloudflare asks for one.
About $5 a month, paid to Cloudflare from your payment method, never to the people who make Civicsmith. You can cancel it in the same place.
Turn on R2 storage
R2 is where your team's Civicsmith keeps the documents and evidence your members collect, each exactly as it was captured.

words.en: Why does my team need its own Cloudflare account?

So that nobody else holds your team's work: the people who make Civicsmith keep none of it and can't open your account. Whoever can sign in to the account controls your team's Civicsmith, so use an account that belongs to your team, and add a second trusted person to it.
What does it cost, who is paid, and how do we stop paying?

About $5 a month for Workers Paid, and R2 storage beyond the 10 GB Cloudflare includes, all paid to Cloudflare only. Nothing is paid to the people who make Civicsmith. To stop paying, cancel Workers Paid in Cloudflare's dashboard. Your team's Civicsmith stops working when the plan ends, so agree on it as a team first.
What can Civicsmith see and do in our account, and how do we remove it?

The installer can create and update your team's Civicsmith's own programs and storage, and nothing else, and it keeps no access afterward. To remove your team's Civicsmith, use the installer's page, or delete its parts in Cloudflare's dashboard, in Workers & Pages and in R2.
Is our card shared with Civicsmith?
No. Your payment method stays with Cloudflare. The installer never sees it, and the permission you give can't reach billing.
What if we already use Cloudflare?

Use that account if it belongs to your team: your team's Civicsmith is added beside what's already there under its own names, nothing else is changed, and the installer checks there is room. If the account is one person's, open a separate one for the team. If it already holds a Civicsmith, the installer says so and asks what you'd like to do.

words.en: What if we get stuck?

Close the installer at any step and come back: it opens where you left off, and nothing is lost. Cloudflare's own help pages explain each of its steps, and when something is missing, the installer says exactly what.

words.en: Someone who handed material to your team: what became known about them, who may read it, and what they agreed to publish.
A team is recorded by its short name, the same one the installer accepts: 3 to 40 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, beginning and ending with a letter or a digit. Nothing was recorded.

Your team's Civicsmith has its team recorded already, and it is recorded once: the name travels inside every document the record has signed, so a second name would make those documents name a producer they were not written under. Nothing was changed.
Only one of the team's administrators can set the name it shows the public or the web address it claims. The person signed in here is not one of its active administrators. Nothing was changed.
A display name is the team's own words for itself: some text, at most 120 characters, on one line. It is always shown beside the team's short name and never instead of it. Nothing was changed.

A web address is claimed by its bare domain name, like example.org: no https://, no path and no port. The claim is then checked by reading a file the domain itself serves, and the public sees the domain only while that check passes. Nothing was changed.
Only one of the team's administrators, signed in as themselves, can choose which jurisdiction profiles your team's Civicsmith reads its local facts from. Nothing was changed.
The profiles are chosen as a list, in the order they are to be read, and an empty list means none. What was sent is not a list. Nothing was changed.
Your team's Civicsmith holds no jurisdiction profile by that name, so it cannot read local facts from it. Choose among the profiles it offers. Nothing was changed.
That profile is made up for testing: its facts describe no real place, so no team's Civicsmith reads local facts from it. Nothing was changed.
The assistant's disclosure is recorded as shown only to the member it was shown to, by their own act, never by another member or a machine on their behalf. Nothing was recorded.
Seats are seeded from captures the record holds of Legistar's bodies, persons and office records, and one of them is not named or cannot be read. Nothing was seeded.
Seats are seeded only from Legistar's own lists of bodies, persons and office records, each named where it belongs, and this capture is not the list named. Nothing was seeded.
A shown disclosure is recorded with the member it was shown to and the version of its words. One of them is missing. Nothing was recorded.
A place your team works in is named in plain words: some text, at most 200 characters, on one line. It is kept only in your team's Civicsmith and sent nowhere. Nothing was changed.
Tell the assistant a little about your team first: it drafts only from what you tell it and what your team already holds. Nothing was saved.
The assistant drafts from your answers to its questions: a short list of answers, each at most 1,000 characters. Nothing was saved.
The language your screens are shown in is your own choice, made from your own signed-in session, never by another member or a machine. Nothing was changed.
A language is chosen by its standard tag, like en, es or zh-Hant, and what was sent is not one. Nothing was changed.
The assistant is asked either to draft words your team's language lacks, or to read one kept word back into English, and this request asks for neither. Nothing was sent and nothing was saved.

Translating the screens is done by members, each from their own signed-in session. The assistant and other machines can draft a translation for a member to check, and can never grant, keep, confirm, undo or mark one. Nothing was changed.
Only the administrators, and members an administrator has asked to translate the screens into this language, can work on its words. You have not been asked for this language. Nothing was changed.
Each word on the screens is known by its key in the list of the interface's words, and that key is not in the list your team's Civicsmith holds. Nothing was changed.
The assistant drafts only the words your team has not yet translated into this language, and this word already has a kept translation. Change a kept word by keeping a new one. Nothing was sent.
The words to draft are named by their keys: a list of at most 100 different keys, or none to draft the first words still missing. What was sent is not such a list. Nothing was sent.

There is nothing for the assistant to draft: every word asked for is either translated already or an official name, which is shown as it is with its official translation where one is published. Nothing was sent.
The draft named is not one the assistant drafted for this word in this language, so it cannot be kept from. Keep the word as you typed it, or choose its draft. Nothing was changed.
A translated word is one line of 1 to 2,000 characters, and it keeps every placeholder in braces, like {name}, exactly as the English has them, so the screen can fill them in. Nothing was changed.
Only a protected word kept with changes, or typed without the assistant's draft, waits for a second check, and this word is not waiting for one. Nothing was changed.
A protected word is checked a second time by someone other than the member who kept it: another member asked to translate this language, or an administrator. Nothing was changed.
This word has not been read back into English for its current text, so an administrator cannot yet confirm it. Read it back into English first, then confirm. Nothing was changed.
This word has never been translated into this language, so there is nothing to undo: members see it in English. Nothing was changed.
Only a translation members are shown can be marked as looking wrong, and this word shows no translation in this language yet. Nothing was recorded.
A note on a translation that looks wrong is optional, and when given it is at most 500 characters. Nothing was recorded.

Explanations open either promptly or on a longer pause, and what was sent is neither. Nothing is ever hidden at either. Nothing was changed.
A logo is a PNG or JPEG picture of at most 200 KB, or nothing to remove it. What was sent is not one. Nothing was changed.

Your team's declared stake says, in its own words, what your team itself has at stake in the matters it works on: some text, at most 1,000 characters, on one line, or nothing to clear it. It is carried on everything your team sends or publishes from now on. Nothing was changed.

A duty is one of three things: an obligation (something owed), a prohibition (something not to be done) or a power (something an office may do). This one is none of them. Nothing was written.
An obligation names who owes it: a registered office or body, an organization acting for a public body, or a person a law binds. None was named. Nothing was written.
An obligation binds a person only where a law or a court binds them by name or role (a filer, a registrant). Cite the held law or order and say the name or role it binds. Nothing was written.

An organization outside government owes a public obligation only when it acts for a public body under a law, contract, franchise or grant. The record holds no such line from this organization to a public body. Record that line, with its citation, first. Nothing was written.
An obligation owed by an organization outside government names the office that enforces it, which is where a concern about it is addressed. None was named. Nothing was written.

An obligation says where it comes from: a held law or standard, a court's order or a report's recommendation, a measured practice, or what it must precede. This source is none of these. Nothing was written.
The part of the law named is not a part the record holds for that standard. Name a section the standard holds. Nothing was written.
The version of the law named is not one the record holds for that instrument. Name a held version. Nothing was written.

The repeating schedule could not be read. It is written as a recurrence rule of the supported kind (weekly, monthly or yearly), with its first date. Nothing was written.
A due date rests on one of four things: a rule the law sets, the body's own commitment, the event it must precede, or the team's own window. This is none of them. Nothing was written.
An obligation never holds an amount of money. A payment it requires cites the money facts the record holds. Remove the amount and cite the facts. Nothing was written.

An obligation arising in a proceeding or report names a registered proceeding or a captured document the record holds. This one names neither. Nothing was written.
A reported status quotes a passage of a captured document the record holds. The passage named is not held. Nothing was written.

An occurrence is met, met late, overdue, pending, discharged or undetermined. This state is none of them. Nothing was written.

Money is set against a prohibition or a threshold whose terms cite money facts and name the funds or bodies they cover. This obligation is not one. Nothing was computed.
Powers are read for an office. The subject named is not a registered office. Nothing was read.
An obligation holds what the record holds, never a working hypothesis: a hypothesis id was found in one of its fields. Remove it. Nothing was written.
An obligation never stores its due date: the date is computed from its rule, trigger and calendar each time it is read. Remove the due date. Nothing was written.
A recorded state of an occurrence, and a version of an obligation, are never changed or removed once written; a later record stands beside them. Nothing was changed.

A policy's review date is read from the policy's own words, and those words must state one whole calendar date. These do not (a placeholder, a month without its day, or more than one date): they are kept as written and never completed. Nothing was written.

A policy's review date, and its review cycle, are cited from a passage of that policy's own text the record holds. The passage named is not held, or is not part of that policy's text. Nothing was written.
The uses of a power are read for a power: something an office may do. This obligation is not one. Nothing was read or written.
The obligations arising in documents are read for 1 to 200 captured documents, each named by its fingerprint (sha256). Nothing was read.

This asks how strongly one question is answered, and no question was named. There is no default question here and there must not be one.
That is not a question, so there is nothing here to say how strongly it is answered. Only a question carries readings of the evidence, and only a reading has a strength.

Say which reading of the evidence to measure, or say which project is asking so that the reading it stands on can be used. There is no default reading, because a strength reported for a reading nobody meant is a number about something else.

No reading by that name belongs to this question, or this project has not said which reading it stands on. An empty answer here would say the question rests on nothing when the truth is that nobody has pointed at anything yet.

One of the words used to say which readings to count is not one this record knows. The set is closed on purpose: a strength that quietly counted readings nobody recognizes would be a number no reader could check.

Nobody has adopted that reading, so it is not what this record answers with. You can still see what it would come to — ask for it as a what-if by saying which kinds of reading to count — and the answer will say on its face that that is what it is.

This answer tried to report one overall figure for a question, and there is no such figure. How well the documents were captured and how firmly they connect to the subject are two separate measurements over two separate things, and averaging them or picking one would state something neither of them says.

This answer did not say which readings it counted, and a strength separated from that is a misreading waiting to happen. Every answer here says on its face whether it is the record's own or a view somebody constructed.
More kinds of reading were named than this record has. The bound is said here rather than applied quietly, so nothing is dropped without you being told.
This asks whether the groups of reasons behind one question share a source, and no question was named. There is no default question here and there must not be one.
That is not a question you can read here, so it has no reasons to group. Only a question rests on reasons, and a question you may not see answers exactly as one that does not exist.

The grouping of reasons could not be read. Send it as a list of groups, each group a list of the positions of the reasons in it, or as groups each carrying a name and its positions. Every group needs at least one reason and a name no other group has.
The grouping names a reason this question does not have. It was not dropped quietly, because an answer about groups the question does not hold would be an answer about something else.
One reason was put in two groups. Each reason belongs to exactly one group, because a reason shared by two groups would make them share a source by construction.
Some of this question's reasons are in no group. A grouping covers every reason, as a written reading does, so that what is checked here is what would be written.
This question rests on more reasons than a written reading may hold, so a grouping of all of them could not be written and is not checked. The bound is said here rather than applied quietly.
Both a written reading and a proposed grouping were named. This answers for one of them at a time, and which one was meant is not something to guess, so name only the one you want.
No reading by that name belongs to this question, so there are no written groups of it to check. Nothing was substituted for it.

A standard of evidence is stated in the grades the record uses, A to D, one for how the documents were captured and one for how firmly they connect. One of the two given is not a grade. Nothing was changed.

A standard of evidence for the whole team is set with a reason: say in your own words why the team works to this standard, in at most 2,000 characters. The reason is kept with it and shown wherever it is read. Nothing was changed.

Ratifying puts a finding into the published record under a member's signature, and the member whose key signed it has to be the one who does it. The credential that asked here is an assistant's: it can prepare the finding and lay out what will be signed, and it cannot carry the signature in for you. Sign in and ratify it yourself.

Ratifying a case commits the team's own assertions about it — its scope, its completeness, its position on the people it concerns — under a member's signature. The credential that asked here is an assistant's: it can assemble the case document, and it cannot be the one who commits it. Sign in and ratify it yourself.

Ratifying puts a finding into the published record under a member's signature, and it is delivered by that member signed in as themselves. The credential that asked here is one of the operator's access tokens for your team's Civicsmith, not a person: a valid signature does not change that, because the credential that carries it in decides when the record changes. Sign in as the member whose key signed it and ratify it there.

Ratifying a case commits the team's own assertions about it under a member's signature, and it is delivered by that member signed in as themselves. The credential that asked here is one of the operator's access tokens for your team's Civicsmith, not a person, and a valid signature does not change that. This finding rests, directly or through another finding, on a member's firsthand observation recorded before the record stopped writing its author's name into the observation's own files, so it is not published. Rest the finding on a newer observation of the same thing, or publish it without that observation in its basis.

A finding in this case rests, directly or through another finding, on a member's firsthand observation recorded before the record stopped writing its author's name into the observation's own files, so the case is not published: that name would be published whatever level its author chose. This asks the record to stand behind something without saying what it rests on. Say what that is first — what the question is grounded in, what you personally observed, or why a settled thing is being changed — and the record carries it beside the claim, in your name, so a later reader can go and disagree with it. If the honest answer is that nothing supports it yet, write that down rather than inventing something: a stated absence is a real answer here, and an empty basis reads as one nobody checked.

A citation is the address of something somebody who was not here can go and read. Without one, what you have written can only be checked by you, and the record would be claiming more than it can show. Name where the source is published or held — if it is not public, say who holds it and how it was seen, which is still an address and is still checkable.

This says the text came from a machine but not which one, or through how many hands. A scanned document can pass through a scanner, a reader and a clean-up pass before anyone sees it, and each one can change what it says — so the record keeps the whole sequence rather than a single word for it.
Nothing here says where this text came from. Text with no stated origin looks exactly like text a publisher typed, and the difference is the whole reason this record is worth trusting.
One of the steps that produced this text is not readable as a step.
One step in this text's history is of a kind the record does not know. It cannot tell whether that step produced the text or checked it, and those are very different things, so it will not guess.
This says a machine read the text but not which machine. Two readers of the same scan disagree, and knowing which one produced a line is what lets anybody check it later.

This step claims the text became more reliable by being processed further. Cleaning up a garbled line makes it easier to READ, not more likely to be what the page actually said — so a later step can only ever be as trustworthy as what it was given.

This confidence figure is the machine's own opinion of itself. A reader that measures how clearly each character resolved is saying something checkable; a model asked how sure it is will answer confidently either way, and that number cannot be used as a threshold. Where an engine reports no confidence, the record says so plainly instead.
The confidence on this region is not readable. Note that saying "this engine reports no confidence" is a real answer here — an absent one is not the same thing.

Attesting is a person saying they compared this text against the image of the page and it matches. The credential that asked here is an automated one: it can run the reader and lay the two side by side, and it cannot be the one who says they agree. Sign in and attest it yourself.

An attestation has to say how much of the document you checked — this region, this page, or all of it. Checking one table and having that stand behind an entire scanned report is exactly what this record will not do on your behalf.

This step points at the measurement its fidelity rests on, but the pointer is not readable as one. A measurement nobody can look up is not a measurement this record can stand behind — and a broken pointer is worse than none, because it looks like one that works.

This step says how faithful a conversion of the document, or an AI's reading of a page, was, but nobody has measured that. When a site hands us its own converted copy of a file, or an AI reads a scan, the record cannot tell what was changed or misread until it has compared the result against the original — so until then it says "not yet determined" rather than giving a grade it has not earned.

This says how faithful a member's own typing of the page is. Nobody grades their own transcription: what a member typed stays "not yet determined" until a different member checks it against the page and says it matches.
