Civicsmith works the strength out from these answers. Once the strength has been shown, a change needs a reason, and the strength before and after is kept beside it.
Accepts this reading as a sound account of what supports the question. A project can then stand on it. Recorded with your name and the date.
Hides this reading from the list. Nothing is deleted: it stays on the record, and anyone can show the hidden readings again.
Marks this reading as one the team is weighing, with a reason. It is not yet accepted, so no project can stand on it.
Rejects this reading, with a reason. It stays on the record, rejected, and can be weighed again later.
Takes back the last decision on this reading, with a reason, so it is weighed again.
Makes this accepted reading the one the project stands on, with a reason. The question does not change; only the project's choice does, and the earlier choice stays on the record.

Picks which mention of them on this page the record reads as the one that connects them: where they are named on the point that matters. Until a member chooses, Civicsmith takes the strongest-graded mention. Your choice is dated and attributed; a later choice replaces it.
Stops using this copy in new work, with a reason. Questions that cite it are told.
Has an independent timestamp service certify that this exact copy existed by now: a timestamp over its fingerprint. It adds no signature of yours and says nothing about whether the copy is true.

Says this name refers to a person the record already follows, with how sure you are (a grade) and why. It is shown as a claim, "claimed the same person, grade B, because…"; the records are linked, never merged, and anyone can see the reason or withdraw it with theirs.
Keeps asking this as new documents arrive; new matches reach your queue once, as a list.
Records a fact about this person from the passage: a position, a credential, an interest. It cites the passage.
Records a dated fact from the passage, citing it, for the timeline.
Works out a due date from the law and the dates, showing each day counted and each holiday skipped. It proposes the date; a member confirms it.

Switches one use on or off for this account: asking, drafting, working through checks and plans, standing questions, suggestions, or exploring (No, Ask every day, Yes). An act this account would pay for, with its use off, stops; it never moves to another account.
Sets or removes one limit on this account: overall, for one use, or for each member's use, in dollars (estimated, API keys only), tokens or calls, a day or a month. It binds this account only.
Holds an Anthropic API key for this project, sealed and never shown again. Switched on, it pays for members' acts in the project, before their own accounts or the team's key.
Makes your own Claude sign-in the project's account, allowed only while you are its only member. If another member joins, it stops serving the project at once and you are told.
Turns the project's account on or off without removing it. While it is off, members' own accounts, then the team's key, serve in the project.
Removes the project's account. Members' own accounts, then the team's key, serve in the project from then on.
Records that you have read what the project's key means, before the first act it pays for.
Keeps this project's material away from AI, for every use or the ones you choose, with a reason every member sees. It binds every account, whoever pays.

Makes this project a counsel matter, your own project, or neither, with your reason. A counsel matter's correspondence and dates are seen only by its members and never published; your own project is hidden and yours alone.
Chooses which acts in this project need a second member's approval before they are sent: a kind of action, a tier, or anything addressed to the public. Your reason is kept with the setting.
Drafts a rule of your team's own, a deadline or a legal fact, from the captured document that states it. It applies only after another member confirms it.
Confirms a rule another member drafted, after checking it against its source. For a Tier 2 or Tier 3 matter you state your professional qualification.
Withdraws one of your team's own rules, with your reason. It is kept, and no longer applied.
Gives you the rule, its source and its confirmation as one exact file, to send to whoever keeps your places' shared rules.
Proposes an obligation from the body's own reply or report: a promise it made, or a response the report requires, quoting it. A member adopts it before it is tracked.
Lists the obligations adopted from these documents, and whether each is met.
Shows the routes your places' rules and your team give for this kind of action, each with the law or rule it cites. Legal information, not legal advice.
Changes when your standing question stops being asked again.
Records, in your team's own words, what it stands to gain or lose. It is shown beside your team's name wherever its work is published.
Lists the dates proposed for this action's clock that no member has adopted yet: each with its rule, its basis and who or what proposed it. Adopting one is a separate act.
Shows administrators how the website key and the join link are set, and every change to them, with who made it and when. Never the key or the link itself.
Asks the assistant to point out sentences that read as a claim of breach, a policy position, an ask for your team, or naming staff. It never rewrites them; you decide.
Asks the assistant to draft a documentation of what happened from the record, labeled as its draft until you make it yours.
Asks the assistant to propose how the reply bears on each claim, labeled as its proposal until you lay it out yourself.
Runs every publication check on this case and holds it, checked and unsigned, until it is signed. Nothing is published.
Shows whether this case's check still holds, and if not, why.
Checks your own text, sentence by sentence, against the record: supported, not supported, or contradicted. Only in your own project, and only you see it.
Links a later act of the same office, found compliant, as what corrected an act found noncompliant. Undoing the link needs a reason.
Records a change the matter brought about, in your words, with the evidence for it.
Puts an outcome (a success, a correction by the office, or a harm addressed) into the case's next edition. It is published when that edition is signed.
Records that what you sent was received by them, or served on them, how and when. A deadline may count from it.
Makes this action confidential, or not, with your reason. A confidential action is seen inside the team and never published; the change applies to what is published from now on.
Records a promise your team made to a person, such as an embargo or anonymity, or ends one.
Lists your team's other open actions with the same office. It is information, never a block.
Lays out the reply claim by claim: for each, whether it brings new evidence, disputes without evidence, or doesn't address it.
Proposes a claim-by-claim layout of the reply, labeled as a proposal and kept apart until a member lays it out.
Records that a project or a matter in a plan arose from this reply.
Records pressure that arrived outside any action, such as a letter, post or call. A legal threat can carry a litigation hold.
Records that you sent the litigation hold notice, with a copy or your account of how. It records no recipient and nothing about any member.
Records that a partner organization approved the same text in its own copy. Their copy must match word for word.
Gives the second approval this project requires before sending. Only a member other than the first approver can give it.
Stops pursuing this escalation, with your reason. It is never recorded as ended or as a success, and it can be reopened where it stopped. Unlike pausing, it does not come back on its own.
Asks the assistant for a first draft of this status report from the plan's items. The draft is labeled machine work, each line cites what it rests on, and nothing is saved until you save it as yours.
Starts a run on your own Claude sign-in, for you alone: checking this, or planning how to look into it. What it produces is labeled machine work and changes nothing until a member acts on it.
Reopens an escalation your team stopped pursuing, at the stage where it stopped, with your reason.
Sets this scenario aside, with your reason. It is kept whole, and can be restored.
Brings a set-aside scenario back, with your reason.
Pauses this plan, with your reason and, if you like, a day to look at it again. What it set running carries on.
Resumes a paused plan, with your reason.
Records, in your team's own words, the outcome it wants for this matter.
Takes this item's to-dos for yourself. Nobody assigns anybody; you choose.
Records that this plan set this watch running, so the plan knows to ask whether to keep it when it closes.
Keeps this watch until a date you choose, or stops it now.
Sets or removes the date to stop following this.

Has the assistant read up to 8 pages of this document that Civicsmith's own reading couldn't make out. The account that pays for your acts here pays, within its limits. Its words arrive labeled as the assistant's reading and stay undetermined until a member checks a passage against the page; the page images stay as they are.
Types the words of a page yourself, from its image. Your typing is labeled as yours, and a second member can check it against the page.
Lets the assistant explore today, on this account, what it said is worth exploring. Without a yes today, it doesn't.

Changes the handle the record shows on your work. Members see your earlier handle beside it, and no one else can ever take it. Allowed until your work first appears in a published case; after that it is fixed.
Checks, as you type, whether this handle can be used in the team: free, already taken, or using characters a handle can't have. It never says who has a handle.
Withdraws a mark on a photo, with your reason, for example when it covers what the finding shows. The withdrawal is recorded beside the mark; the public copy follows the marks that stand.
Marks anyone in a photo who is not part of a finding, and any number plate, so the copy a published case carries shows them obscured, labeled. The original stays inside the team.
Holds this requirement as a standard the city set itself, so questions can test the city against it.
Reads this figure into a money fact, with its stage and period, citing where it came from.
Says what a table's columns are, so its figures can be counted through a calculation rather than one by one.
Sets the team's bar: how strong an answer must be before the team relies on it, in every project that sets no bar of its own.

Sets this project's own bar, with your reason: the strength each of its questions is measured against. It never changes the team's bar and holds nothing back; it shows how far each answer is from the bar.
Brings a question from elsewhere in your team into this project, with a note on why. The project draws on it; the question stays where it is, and is not copied.
Ties what you recorded at one drawn report to the spot-check: repaired, not repaired, or could not tell. It counts toward the estimate only for a report in the draw.
Lists the questions this project draws on, its own and those drawn in from elsewhere.
Lists the projects you may see.
Invites a member into this project, so they can see and work on it.
Joins this project to see and work on it.
Asks this project's owners to let you in, with a word on why if you like. They grant or decline it; you see their answer, and you can withdraw your request while it waits.
Withdraws your request to join this project. Its owners no longer see it, and you can ask again later.
Grants or declines a member's request to join your project, with a word if you like. Granting invites them; they join when they choose. Administrators see requests and answer none.
Checks your password, then does what you asked, once. Nothing else changes.
Opens a plan: what the team could do about what it found, its options and what each would take.
Removes this citation from the question or the case, with the reason kept. It can be reinstated.
Puts a removed citation back on the question or the case.
Narrows the question to what the record can answer, with the reason. The wider question is kept.
Records the team's answer to the question, from what it rests on. It can be withdrawn later, with a reason.
Takes a finding back from concluded, with a reason, so the team can work on it again and publish a correction as the next edition.
Withdraws the question's answer, with a reason, for example after new evidence.
Changes the words of a hunch, with your reason. The earlier words stay on the record.
Takes a hunch back, with your reason. It stays on the record but no longer counts as a hunch.
Ends this question and carries it on as two new ones, with your reason. Every passage goes to at least one of them. This cannot be undone.
Records that you looked again at a change under this question, and what you decided. That change stops being listed until something moves again.
Lists what this question rests on that has changed since it was written.
Asks whether this standard was in force on a day you choose, and why.
Keeps a hunch beside the question, labeled as yours. A hunch is never evidence and never moves an answer.
Shows one matter followed through a progression: each step in order with the documents threaded to it, how sure the chain is, and any finding.
Shows a progression: its steps, what each needs before it, how soon, whether it is required, its basis, and every version.
Declares a progression, or a new version of one: its steps and their basis. A revision needs a citation; the old version stays.
Places a document the team holds on a step of a matter it concerns, with the document's own date. Each threading is a new version, so nothing is overwritten.
Records why a required step was lawfully skipped: the document that shows it, your reason and the citation. The finding then reads as a lawful skip.
Shows every step of every matter this document is threaded to, with any finding there.
Lists the team's themes, newest first, or what one theme gathers: what was placed in it, then its hunches apart. Documents you cannot open are left out.
Shows the statements in force for the whole team or for one project, who adopted them and why, what the set does not enforce, and a number that identifies the lens.
Puts a saved, offered bias set in force for the whole team (an administrator) or for one project (an owner), with your reason. It records the revision you adopted; adopting again replaces it.
Reads another organization's policy and proposes statements from it, with the sentences it left out and why. It saves, offers and adopts nothing.
Shows the record of work made under an earlier lens: the lens then and now, and every settlement so far.
Settles work made under an earlier lens, with your reason that the change does not bear on it. Your name and reason stay in the record and cannot be taken back.
Declares a theme for the whole team: its name and the test something must meet to belong. A theme is a lens, never evidence.
Places this document or passage in a theme, with an optional note saying why. At a hunch, it confirms the hunch and keeps who proposed it.
Proposes this document or passage for a theme as a hunch: it shows apart and counts for nothing until another member places it.
Takes a placement out of a theme (the member who placed it, or an administrator) or rejects a hunch (any member). Your reason is required and stays on record.
Asks a member with the right expertise to check this, for example an accountant for figures.
Asks in plain words. The assistant answers only from what your team holds and says where it looked.
Shows how this answer was counted: the rule it applies, the rows it counted and the method, so you can check it rather than rely on it.
Stops asking this question on a schedule.
Asks the assistant to work on what this screen shows. Its results are labeled as machine work and become the team's only when a member accepts them.
Asks the assistant for suggestions here. Each is labeled as its suggestion, for you to adopt or ignore.
Stops the assistant's run. What it produced so far stays labeled as its draft.
Opens this person's page: positions, career and interests, each dated and cited.
Withdraws a claim that two records are the same person, with a reason.
Withdraws a statement that an office keeps the records on a subject or is responsible for it, with a reason. The statement is not deleted: the page still shows that it was there.
Follows a public register (licenses, filings) and tells you when an entry for this changes.
Removes a recorded value for good where the law or a court requires it. It cannot be undone by anyone; a marker stays where it was.
Records an event on the timeline from a cited source or your own testimony.
Adds who took part in an event, by name or by role.
Links two events, for example one caused or answered another, citing why.
Starts a money trail: the figures and transfers that follow one sum through the city's funds.
Includes this figure in the trail, with the reason.
Leaves this figure out of the trail, with the reason, so others see why.
Compares two sources' figures for the same thing and shows where they differ.
Compares what was committed with what was paid, period by period.
Shows what authorized this money: the vote, contract or rule, each cited.
Works out a figure from the record, with its method shown so anyone can repeat it.
Draws a random sample to check by hand, recorded so the draw can be repeated.
Binds your spreadsheet to the record, so its inputs come from cited documents and it can be recomputed.
Ties one of the spreadsheet's inputs to a cited place in the record.
Records that a second member checked the calculation, with what they found.
Accepts the result as a computed fact the team can cite.
Looks for chains of links between two people or organizations, each step cited and graded.
Uses a ready-made search, such as "money from a vendor to an official".
Checks each step of a chain against its sources and grades it.

Says, in your own words and under your name, that this document and another one your team holds are connected. It is kept apart from the connections the record derives and is not treated as established.
Adds a party to the proceeding by its role, citing where it appears.
Reads this document again with OCR, which looks for words in the page images, and replaces this copy's current reading. The original file stays as captured.
Confirms, as a second member, that a page another member typed matches the page, with a note of what you compared. It raises what the typing can claim; the typist's own confirmation never counts.
Checks the evidence this copy carries about where it came from and records, under your name, whether its route to your team can be shown. The document does not change.
Reports, with your reason, that the record matched a mention in this document to the wrong subject. The report is kept beside the match; the match itself is not changed.
Holds an order's requirements as obligations, so the team can check whether they are met and by when.
Links a decision to the law or order it interprets, citing the passage.
Confirms the due date, so reminders and the queue use it.
Reminds you on a date you choose. Only you see it.
Adopts a proposed standard as one the team holds the city to.
Relates the standard to the law it comes from, citing the passage.
Adds a matter to the plan: one problem the team wants to act on, with your reason.
Adds an option: one thing the team could do, with what it would take.
Asks the assistant for options. They wait in the tray, labeled, until a member adopts one.
Adopts a suggested option into the plan as the team's own.
Chooses an option or declines it, with the reason kept on the plan.
Lays out what might happen if an option is taken, step by step.
Records how a checkpoint turned out, so the plan reflects what happened.
Shows what starting this option would do and anything that would stop it, before you start.
Closes the plan, with how it ended. It stays readable.
Shows only the findings at or above the strengths you chose. It changes only what you see, and the page says it is a view you constructed.
Takes your minimum away and shows the whole case again.
Prints the whole case: every finding open with its sources listed, and the signature line. A print of a filtered view says so at its foot.
Makes a file of this copy on your device, stamped on every page. A file can't be recalled, unlike a link, which your team can end.
Registers the public key a member gave you as theirs, so they can sign for the team. The record shows you did it.
Starts the action: the team begins doing this option, from here to the send.
Prepares the text that will be sent, from the team's template or a labeled draft.
Prepares the filing with what the venue requires.
Approves this exact text for sending. Changing it afterwards needs approving again.
Keeps the text you approved as the first draft of a template for your team. Nothing is offered to members until the team approves it.
Records that you sent it, when and how. Civicsmith never sends for you; reply deadlines count from here.
Chooses the office it goes to, by role, so it reaches whoever holds the post that day.
Starts the records request as an action the team follows to its reply.
Chooses the records law the request goes under. It decides the deadline.
Moves the action to its next stage, with what happened.
Records a reply or letter received, with its date, so deadlines and the timeline follow.
Ends the hold, with your reason. What it covered may be purged again on the team's usual schedule, and this cannot be undone. Any member who can see the action or the case can release it.
Marks a reply as pressure (a threat, a demand to stop), kept on the record.

Records a litigation hold with your reason. While it lasts, what it covers is not purged, a scheduled publication of it does not go out, and the doorbell clears nothing. Any member who can see the action or the case may place one.
Assembles a plain notice from the record: the place the hold is for, your reason, the date and the kinds of material to keep. Nothing is sent.
Assembles what the record holds on this action as one packet for your team's lawyer, as it stands today, with your reason kept beside it. It is never published and never filed.
Opens an escalation: taking the matter to a higher body, with the reason.
Moves the escalation to its next level, with what happened.
Decides not to escalate at all, with the reason kept, so the team knows it chose not to. To keep an escalation open but stay at its current stage, use Hold at this stage instead.
Ends the escalation, with how it ended.

Records your team's judgment of whether an office's act met a rule: compliant, noncompliant or unclear, with what it rests on. It is never edited; a mistake is put right by a new determination that replaces it, with a reason.
Records what a breach did and to whom, as a figure the record supports or as your own assessment with its reason.
Replaces one recorded consequence with a corrected one, with your reason. The earlier version stays readable.
Records, with evidence and a reason, whether one consequence was addressed or not.
Attaches an action of your team to the stage the escalation stands at, with your reason.
Holds the escalation at its current stage instead of moving to the stage now proposed, with your reason. The proposal stays in view and the escalation stays open.
Pauses the whole escalation: no stage is proposed and no step is asked of you until you resume it. A deadline already running keeps running.
Takes a paused escalation up again at the stage where it stopped.
Records how you read the government's response at the response stage: complied, partly, denied or no response, with your reason.
Prepares the case's draft from the team's answers and their sources.
Asks the assistant to draft "what changed" since the last edition, labeled as its draft.
Acknowledges what the case does not cover, so readers are told.
Names a person in the case with the reason it must, under the team's rules for naming people.
Shares the draft with named people outside the team until a date. You can stop sharing at any time.
Stops sharing the review copy at once.
Comments on the draft, for the case's owner to read.
Checks the case is ready to publish and lists anything that would stop it.
Asks a trusted time-stamp service, and an outside archive, to confirm a document again. It shows the document existed by now, not when it was captured.
Adds your signed account of when and how you captured a document. Only the member who captured it can add one, and it cannot be removed.
Shows what must be disclosed in the case, such as members' ties that concern it.
Signs this edition, its findings and their evidence with your key, and publishes it now. Readers can check each signature without the team.
Publishes the signed edition for anyone to read. It can never be unpublished; corrections come as a new edition.
Moves the time this signed edition becomes public. The signature stands; Civicsmith checks again at the new time.
Keeps this signed edition unpublished. You can choose a time again, or sign a new edition.
Publishes at a set time. Civicsmith checks again then, and does not publish if anything changed since signing.
Checks the case's signature and that it matches what the team signed, without the team's help.
Reads the published case.
Imports another team's published case and recreates it here, finding by finding.
Accepts what recreated, with a reason, so your team can rely on it.
Withdraws your team's acceptance, with a reason; it stays in the history, and work that relied on it gets a fresh look.
Flags an issue in the imported case, kept within your team.
Watches the other team's docket for corrections to the case.
Files a docket entry: a correction, withdrawal or court order about a published case.
Posts the entry to the public docket, where readers see it beside the case.
Moves material handed in at the doorbell into the record, where it can be vouched for.
Discards material handed in, with a reason.
Records what is known about who handed this in, without exposing them.
Sets, changes or removes how this project's success is measured, with your reason. The project then counts its own progress from its documents.
Decides one proposal for this objective: adopt it, open a question from it, defer it or dismiss it. Deferring or dismissing it records your reason.
Records what a team, a project or a member holds itself to. A team's aspiration is declared by an administrator.
Records that this project does not hold to the team's aspiration, with your reason, which every member can read.
Adds what was tried and why it went nowhere to an aspiration, with your name and the date. It is never removed.
Retires an aspiration and records what pursuing it taught. It and its dead ends stay readable, and it cannot be brought back.
Opens a goal: what it pursues and what limits it, optionally under an aspiration.
Records that this project's objective serves a goal, with your name and the date.
Closes a goal with your reason. It stays readable with its projects and cannot be reopened.
Hands the material to the team. You need no account; tell them only what you choose.
Lists the other material that came in with the same secret phrase, oldest first. It shows that the knocker is the same one; it never says who they are.
Records your yes, or your taking it back, for one detail the team asked to publish about you, using your secret phrase. Agreeing is permanent for what is published under it.
Records one thing that became known about a source, how it became known and who knows it, with your evidence. An entry is never edited; a later one takes its place.
Records that the source agreed to one detail being shown to one audience. It is permanent for anything published under it.
Records that the source took their agreement back. It binds only what is published afterward; what was already published stays published.
Says, with your evidence, that a source is a person your team follows. The two records are not merged; the claim is shown to the members you list.
Writes down something you were told or suspect, and where it might be found. A lead is somewhere to look, never evidence; only you can read it until you share it.
Opens a lead with every look recorded against it and the projects it was shared with.
Records that you looked into a lead, what you found and where you looked. It is kept with your name.
Shows your lead to the participants of one project, with your reason. It cannot be taken back.
Lists every address your team watches that you may see, including the ones with no schedule, with when each was last checked and when it is next due.
For administrators: stops all watching until it is resumed, or resumes it. While paused, no address is checked and nothing is gathered.
Reads what is due now, the addresses and the sweeps, as a prompt you can run by hand.
Lists the sweeps you may see, with who ratified each, when it runs next and what it has kept.
Item
The item's own title, as your team holds it. Open it to read it.
Kind
What sort of item it is: a document, a question, an action or a case.
State
Where the item stands in your team's work. Rest on a state to see what it means and what it allows.
Updated
The day the item last changed in your team's record, not the day it was written.
Member
Each member by the handle the record shows, and whether they are an administrator.
May do
What each member may do here, as the administrators set it: add and revise work, start projects, sign and publish cases. An administrator may do all of it, and also looks after the team's Civicsmith.
Expertise
What a member says they know, such as accounting or engineering, so others can ask them to check work in that field. Each member declares it in their account; an administrator can confirm it.
Figure
What the amount is, in the words of its source: a transfer, a charge, a payment, a grant.
From
Who or which fund paid, as the source writes it. The payer is part of the figure itself, never guessed from somewhere else.
To, where it went
Who or which fund received the money, as the source writes it. "Not stated in this source" means this source does not say; record it from another source that does, citing the passage.
When it moved

The day the money actually moved, taken from the event the figure is tied to and the passage that dates it. A budget figure did not move, so it shows when it was adopted instead. Undetermined means no source the team holds gives the day; it is never guessed from the accounting period.
Stage

How far along the money was when the source counted it: adopted (budgeted), committed (promised by contract), or actual (spent; "paid" when the source shows the payment). Figures at different stages are compared, never added.
Period
The accounting period the source counts the amount in, such as a fiscal year, which need not match the calendar year. It is not the date the money moved: that is in When it moved.
Amount
The amount exactly as the source states it. A rounded amount ("about $2 million") keeps its rounding.
Source
The document the figure was read from, with its capture grade: how sure the team is that the copy is what the office published. Click the mark for the document.
In this trail?
Whether this figure counts in the trail's comparison, and the member's reason for including it or leaving it out. A figure left out stays listed, with why.
Kind
The kind of attempt that was turned away. Each counts attempts, not people.
This period
How many of this kind in the period you are looking at.
Usual
Your team's own median for the same length of time over the four weeks before. Far above it is what makes a period Raised or High.
Busiest hour
The hour with the most of this kind, and its count.
English

The words as Civicsmith ships them. Protected marks words that carry a ruling and need a second member's check before a translation is used; Local name marks a name kept as it is, with its explanation translated.
Español
The translation members see. A shaded cell is a draft, not yet shown to anyone.
Where it came from
Whether the translation came with a Civicsmith release, was typed by a member, or started as the assistant's draft, and whether it still needs its second check.
Click to sort the rows by this column; click again to reverse. Sorting changes only your view, never the record.
Set up and claim
Check you have what is needed: a Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan ($5 a month, with a payment method) and about twenty minutes.
Civicsmith uses parts of Cloudflare that only the paid plan includes. No Claude account is needed to set up.
Choose your team's short name, then install. It is not the team's name: you choose that next, and can change it.
The short name is the fixed label in your addresses and beside every signature, and can never change. A team that wants to stay unnamed picks one that reveals nothing.
Your team's Civicsmith tests itself as part of installing; the finished panel shows what passed. Allow it to run its file scanner if you are asked.
The test proves it works before anyone relies on it. The installer keeps nothing once it hands over, so the checks are run then, not later.
Save the one-time password somewhere safe, such as a password manager, then continue.
It is shown once, and it is how you become the first administrator. Continuing fills it in; if it is lost before you claim, whoever can sign in to the Cloudflare account can set a new one.
Make it yours: with the one-time password (already filled in if you came straight from the installer), choose your handle and your own password, and claim.
Only the person holding the one-time password can become the first administrator. Once you claim, it is spent.
Open “Your team”: type its name as people should read it, and add its logo if it has one.
The team's name heads everything it publishes and can change at any time; the short name you chose at install stays fixed in addresses and signatures.
If your team has a website of its own, choose “Yes” and verify its address: put the small file Civicsmith gives you on the site.
Readers can then confirm that a published case really comes from your team. The public page names the site, so a team that wants to stay unnamed skips this.
Open “Where your team works”: choose your place, and the languages your members read.
Deadlines, holidays and offices come from these places, never from Civicsmith itself. If yours is not listed, choose Other: everything else works, and you enter due dates yourself.
Open “The officials you deal with”: check the offices and who holds them, then confirm the list. Each is marked with where it came from.
Requests go to offices by role, so correct anything before members rely on it.
Open “Privacy and the law” and read who will see facts about people.
Facts from public documents follow those documents; a project's own notes about a person stay inside the project.
Open “The AI assistant”, read what it is, then choose whether your team uses it. Choosing “No” keeps the team's material away from AI and hides the rest.
Any member may connect their own Claude account unless you keep the material away from AI; then members see who chose it and your reason. Everything works without the assistant.
If your team will pay for the assistant, choose “Your team, with one API key” and paste the key. It is never shown again.
It serves every member with no account of their own; each is told once, before their first question, that it goes to Anthropic under the team's account. Leave it empty and members bring their own.
In “Privacy and the law”, choose whether members are told what a court can reach.
A court order your team cannot defeat can require anything not public to be shown. Some teams want every member told; the explanation is always one tap away.
In “A second administrator”, record who holds the hosting account.
If you are ever unreachable, this is how the team gets back in.
Invite a second administrator, now or later; your first members come after.
With one administrator the team depends on one person. A second means it is never stuck.
Optional: say who your team is. You will come back here when you finish or stop.
It shapes how each member is welcomed. It locks nothing and is never required.
Welcome a new member
Choose your language.
Everything that follows should be in words you read easily. It starts from your device's setting.
Choose a handle and a password.
The record shows your handle on your work. It needn't be your legal name: a known name lends credibility, a pen name shields you, and administrators still know who you are.
This is your team's home: what it is working on, and what is waiting on you.
Come back here whenever you lose your place.
Here is your team's most recent question. Two things to know first: its strength against its project's bar, and "Undetermined".
You will see these everywhere. Every other mark is explained where you meet it, one tap away.
Optional: connect your own Claude account, or skip.
The assistant serves only you, and every journey works without it.
Optional: tell the team about your own ties.
Only you and the administrators see them, and they let a case disclose a tie honestly.
Take a first step: join a project, capture a document, or record what you saw.
One small act is enough to begin. Nothing here has to be done in order.
Publication ceremony
Check what you are publishing: the case, its edition and its scope.
Publishing is permanent. This is the last look before it.
Check each finding's strength against the bar, and anything still open.
A reader sees each finding's strengths. Anything still open is disclosed, never hidden.
Read what the case leaves out, and who acknowledged it.
Saying what a case does not cover is part of its honesty.
Check each person the case names, with the reason they matter to a finding.
A case cannot be signed while any reason is missing.
Check each photo the case relies on: mark anyone in it who is not part of a finding, and any number plate.
The public copy shows them obscured and says so; the original stays inside the team.
Read what will be disclosed: the timeline as it stands, and any calculation that differs or is not tied to the record.
Readers must see what the case could not settle.
Read the team's declared bias as it will appear.
Every published case carries the lens it was made through.
Preview the public page as a stranger will see it.
This is how a reader with no account meets your work.
Confirm you have no undeclared tie to anyone the case concerns, and prepare the edition for signing.
Including anyone paid in its money. Your confirmation goes inside what you sign. A tie disclosed is a strength; one found later is not.
Choose when it becomes public, enter your password again, and sign: your device asks you once to confirm with your key, for the edition, its findings and their evidence together.
Only you can sign, and Civicsmith never sees your key. Publishing is permanent; corrections come as a new edition, never by changing this one.
To publish later, sign now with “Sign and publish at…”, such as when a story citing it runs.
At that time Civicsmith checks again; if anything changed since you signed, it holds the case and tells you. You can cancel or move the time until then.
Get a record
Look first: is the record already public? Search what your team holds and where the office publishes.
Much is public already. A copy from the office's own site holds up better than one found elsewhere.
If you find it, capture it from its address. Then you are done.
Capturing keeps a fingerprinted copy that cannot change under you.
If not, choose the office that holds the records.
The request goes to the office by its role, so it reaches whoever holds the post that day. You will see who that is.
Say plainly what records you want.
A clear description is harder to refuse, or to answer only in part.
Choose the law the request goes under, from your team's places.
The law sets the office's deadline. Where a faster kind of request fits, it is offered.
Read the draft request and edit it until it is yours.
The wizard only drafts. The words that are sent are yours.
Approve the text.
Approving is kept apart from sending, so you can stop between them.
Send it the way the office accepts requests, then record that you sent it.
Sending tells the office what your team is looking at. Recording the send starts the clock.
Confirm the due date worked out from the law. Download it to your calendar if you like.
You can see exactly how it was counted, and challenge it.
Check a claim
Capture the claim where the city made it: a budget, a report to council, a press release.
The claim itself is your first piece of evidence.
Point at the words that make the claim.
Every later step refers back to exactly what was said.
Open the question: do the city's own records support the claim?
A claim cannot be checked; a question can be answered, or shown undetermined.
Pin down what the claim's words mean: what counts, and over what period. If the city never says, record that.
A share means nothing until you know what was counted. A gap is recorded as undetermined, with its reason.
Get the city's own records behind the claim: online, or by request.
The claim should be checked against the city's own data, not anyone's impression.
Work it out with the built-in calculation, or bind your own spreadsheet to the captured records.
The method is shown with the result, so anyone can check it.
Plan a spot-check: a recorded random draw picks which records members visit.
A draw anyone can repeat means no one can say you picked the worst cases.
Members visit and record what they find, with place and date, and a photo where they can take one.
Firsthand checks test whether the records match the street.
Conclude with what the evidence supports, and say what would change it.
A conclusion that names what would change it is one others can trust.
Your first question
What drew you in? A problem you live with, a person, a payment or contract, or something you read.
Any of these is a good start. Civicsmith offers a first step from each.
Say what you want to know, as a question.
A question is something the record can answer: yes, no, or undetermined, and why.
Find or capture a document that bears on it.
Every answer rests on documents anyone could check.
Point at the passage that matters.
Citing a passage, not a whole document, shows exactly what you rely on.
Say whether it supports the question or cuts against it.
Evidence against is kept as carefully as evidence for.
See the question's strength against the project's bar, and what would raise it.
Strength is two grades, never one score: how well the documents are held and how firmly they are linked.
Say who your team is
What kind of team are you? Pick one or more, or describe your own.
It shapes how each member is welcomed. It never limits what anyone can do.
What do you focus on: issues, places, offices or agencies?
New members see your focus first when they choose where to start.
Why does the team exist? Say it in your own words.
Your declared bias can start from what you write here.
Who should see this: members only, or also your public page and the network directory?
Members only is the default. A team that wants to stay unnamed keeps it that way.
Invite a member
Who: a short id for the invitation, and the cover the team knows them by. Not a legal name.
They choose their own handle when they join. The record never needs a legal name; administrators keep the cover so they know who is who.
What they may do. Contributing is the default.
Give only what the person needs; you can change it later.
Send the link yourself. It works once and expires after seven days.
Civicsmith sends no email, so the link reaches them only through you.
Or let people join through your website: create a website key, or turn on the reusable join link.
Anyone let through can see the team's shared work, so each comes with limits and a daily cap.
Update your team's Civicsmith
Read what changes: the signed release notes say what members will see, what administrators will see, and anything an administrator must do.
The notes are signed with the release itself, so what you read is what Civicsmith published.
Choose Update if you hold your team's Cloudflare account. If not, copy the link and pass it to whoever does. Not now and Skip this version are the other choices.
Only Cloudflare's consent, given by the account's holder, lets a new release in. Your team's Civicsmith cannot rewrite itself.
On the installer's page, check the release running and the release chosen, then continue to Cloudflare and allow the update.
If a step stops, your team's Civicsmith keeps running as it was; the stop says what to do.
Connect your Claude account
The assistant is optional. If your team offers its API key, you can use it already; your own account, if you connect one, always comes first.
Your own account serves only you. Everything works without the assistant.
Read what connecting means.
Your questions, and what is read to answer them, go to Anthropic under your own account.
To connect your Claude subscription, open Anthropic's sign-in page, sign in and approve. Or use an API key, or skip.
You sign in on Anthropic's own page; Civicsmith never sees your Claude password. Skipping is a real choice: every journey stays open.
Copy the code Anthropic's page shows you, paste it under "The code from Anthropic's page", and connect with it.
The code is used once and never kept. Your subscription then serves only your own questions, and you can disconnect at any time.
Using an API key instead? Paste it under "Using an API key instead" and connect with it.
Anthropic bills you for each use of your own key; it serves only your questions.
Set a limit on your account, if you want one: for everything or for one use, a day or a month.
It binds only your own account. The team's and a project's limits never bind it.
Choose what your account pays for, and whether the assistant may suggest things without being asked. Suggestions are off unless you turn them on.
Some members want suggestions; others want quiet.
You can disconnect at any time, here: your subscription, or your API key.
Disconnecting removes the sign-in or the key from your team's Civicsmith.
Your ties
List your employer, relatives, and businesses you have an interest in.
A case concerning any of them can then disclose the tie honestly.
Only you and the administrators can see this.
Your ties never appear in a case unless one concerns it, and then only as you choose.
For each tie, choose how a published case discloses it when the case concerns them: naming you by your handle, or as “a member of the team”.
Readers learn of the tie either way; not naming you protects you while keeping the case honest.
Follow a proceeding
Capture a filing, or the court's register page.
The proceeding is registered from what it says about itself.
Register the proceeding from its caption: the court, the number, and a neutral label.
A neutral label keeps your own view out of the record's name for it.
Add the parties by role.
Roles say who is suing, who is sued, and who is deciding.
Follow its register: on a schedule, or by your own capture where the register needs a login.
New filings are flagged, so nothing arrives unseen.
Hold each order's requirements as obligations, with their reply dates.
An order is a standard the office must meet. Its dates go into your queue.
Follow the money
Capture the budget, financial report or contract.
Every figure must point back to where it was printed.
Read just the figures you need, each with its stage and period.
Proposed, adopted, committed and paid are different facts. Mixing them is how money stories go wrong.
Start a money trail.
A trail gathers the figures one question needs.
Include or leave out each item, with a reason.
Your reasons show a reader why the trail adds up the way it does.
Compare two sources of one figure, or what was committed against what was paid.
Differences in basis, period or rounding are named, not hidden.
Build a timeline
Record an event from a cited passage: what, when, and how precisely you know the date.
Every event points at its source. A date you only know roughly is recorded as rough.
Add who took part and in what role: decided, signed, voted.
Roles are what make an event useful to a finding.
Link events: made under, answered, amended.
Links let a reader follow one thread through the record.
Keep a suspected cause as a hunch, never as a fact.
A hunch is marked as yours and is never evidence.
Review the two lanes before the case is signed: what they did, and what we did.
The timeline is frozen into the case when it is signed.
Keep asking this
Choose how often to check, and until when.
An end date is required, so no question runs forever.
The search runs on schedule. With the assistant connected, it reads only what is new, on your account and within your limit.
Without the assistant, new matches arrive as a list for you to read.
The answer reaches your queue once.
Only you see it; it is never shared.
Stop it any time.
Stopping is immediate, and nothing further is checked.
Use another team's case
Import the case into its own read-only project.
Another team's work stays marked as theirs, and cannot be edited.
Civicsmith recreates each finding and calculation from the case file. Watch each one's mark.
Recreated, recreated in part, or did not recreate: you never rely on what you could not check.
Accept what recreated, with a reason.
Accepting names one edition and changes no grade.
Watch the publisher's docket for new editions and corrections.
Anything relying on the case is told when it changes.
Translate the interface
Choose the language.
Civicsmith's own translations come with releases. Your team fills gaps and improves wording.
See the words still untranslated.
A missing word shows in English, never blank.
Where you can reach the assistant, ask it to draft them all. Each is marked "Draft · the assistant's".
Your task becomes finding its errors. Without the assistant, type them yourself.
Read each draft against the English; keep it or correct it.
A word becomes the team's only when a granted member who knows the language keeps it.
A protected word you changed, or typed without a draft, waits for a second check.
A second granted speaker, or an administrator reading the assistant's back-translation, confirms it. Until then members see the English.
Comment for the team
Choose a public comment as the option, and the meeting or comment period it is for.
Choosing records why this option, now.
Start the comment, addressed to the body that holds the meeting.
It goes to the body by role, so it reaches whoever sits there that day.
Choose "For the team" or "As myself", then write what the record shows and what you ask the body to examine or apply. Start from your team's template for a written comment if it has one.
A comment for the team is the team's act. One as yourself is your own notes, never recorded as sent.
Read any sentence pointed out as a policy position: remove it, or comment as yourself.
A comment for the team states facts and asks. A position is a member's to take as themselves.
Approve the text.
Approving is kept apart from sending, so you can stop between them.
Submit it, or read it at the meeting, then record that it was sent.
The record keeps what the team said, and when.
Demand a correction
Choose the demand as the option. Read its advisory first: a demand is a Tier 2 act, and a lawyer's view helps.
A demand can lead to a court; knowing that before starting is part of choosing it.
See what starting does: the window the law gives the body to correct its act, and anything that would stop it.
A demand starts a legal clock. You see it before anything runs.
Start the demand, addressed to the body by role.
The body's holder that day is shown, so you know who will read it.
Write what the body did, the rule it seems to break, and what correcting it would look like. Start from your team's demand template if it has one.
A demand asks the body to correct its own act, so it says exactly what correcting it means.
Rewrite any sentence pointed out as asking for something for your team.
A demand asks nothing for the team. Approval waits until those sentences are gone.
Approve the text.
Approving is kept apart from sending, so you can stop between them.
Send it, then record that you sent it.
Recording it starts the body's window to correct the act.
The window's end goes into your queue.
If the body doesn't correct it, the next stage is ready without anyone remembering.
Take an escalation to its next stage
Read where the escalation stands. Each stage is a question, such as "Did we tell them?" or "What did they say?".
The questions say what each stage needs before the next.
If they replied, record what they said.
The next stage rests on the reply, or on there being none.
Advance to the next stage, or decline to escalate with your reason.
Either way the record keeps why.
If your team is stopping, stop pursuing it, with your reason.
Stopping is never recorded as ended or as a success, and it can be reopened where it stopped.
Set when to look at it again.
An escalation moves only when a member moves it.
Refer it to an oversight body
Choose a referral to the oversight body as the option.
Choosing records why this option, now.
Start the referral, addressed to the oversight body by role.
It goes to the body by role, so it reaches whoever holds it that day.
Write what happened and ask the body to look into it. Start from your team's referral template if it has one.
A referral asks for an examination. It doesn't claim a breach the body hasn't found.
Approve the text.
Approving is kept apart from sending, so you can stop between them.
Send it, then record that you sent it. Say if no reply is owed.
Some oversight bodies don't reply to a referral; saying so keeps a missing reply from being counted against them.
If the referral shouldn't be published, make the action confidential, with your reason.
A confidential action is seen inside the team and never published.
When they reply, record it, with their own words for its status.
Outcomes are kept in the oversight body's own terms.
Pick up a plan
Read where it stands: the matters, what each has reached, and what is due next.
Joining midway starts from what is already true, not from the beginning.
Read the latest status report, if a member saved one, and what changed since.
Each line cites what it rests on, so you can check it.
Take up an item you can do. Nobody assigns anybody: you choose.
Taking it up routes its dates and reminders to you.
Set a reminder for your item.
Your reminder is yours alone.
Start and send
Choose the option, and say when to be reminded.
Choosing records why this option, now.
See what starting does, and anything that would stop it.
Refusals are shown before anything runs.
Start the action, addressed to the office by role.
The office's holder that day is shown, so you know who will read it.
Prepare what is sent: start from your team's template for this kind of action if it has one, or write it yourself. A template or draft is labeled until you make it yours.
The words that leave the team are always a member's.
Approve the text.
Approving is kept apart from sending, so you can stop between them.
Send it, then record that you sent it.
This tells the office what your team is looking at, and starts the clock.
The due date and next checkpoint go into your queue. A next step can wait on the reply.
If no reply comes, the next step is ready without anyone remembering.
